result: In 42 Charité patients with fatigue and exertion intolerance 6 months after mild-moderate COVID-19 (19 meeting CCC), handgrip strength was diminished in most, and several biomarkers were associated with fatigue and PEM severity.
reason: Same measure (handgrip) but a post-COVID clinic cohort with no fatigability or recovery data in the abstract, so a long COVID extension rather than a replication; earlier preprint version of the same study is PPR279456.

result: Of 42 referred patients with persistent fatigue 6 months after mild-moderate COVID-19, 19 met the 2003 Canadian Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS; most were moderately to severely impaired.
reason: Selected clinic cohort with no uninfected comparison, so it measures neither incidence nor population prevalence; it is the 6-month baseline of the Charité CCC cohort in trials-post-covid-course (check for overlap with the cited Charité follow-up).

result: sCD26 was significantly lower only in female ME/CFS patients and not diagnostically useful; in infection-triggered cases low sCD26 correlated with higher alpha1-adrenergic and M3 autoantibodies, activated T cells, CK, LDH and inversely with IL-1b, and in non-infection-triggered cases with orthostatic heart rate and POTS.
reason: Correlates sCD26 with autoantibody levels within patients and does not test whether GPCR autoantibodies are elevated versus controls; no atlas finding covers sCD26/DPP-4 (possible new candidate).

result: In the GETSET RCT (n=211, 78% follow-up at 15 months), the short-term fatigue benefit of guided graded exercise self-help was maintained, but the specialist-care group caught up so arms no longer differed (fatigue p=0.03 and physical function p=0.25, neither significant after multiplicity adjustment); ICER 4802 GBP per QALY.
reason: A separate GET trial using the same self-rated outcomes shows the same pattern of between-group differences vanishing at long-term follow-up, extending the PACE finding to guided self-help.

result: In 11 ME/CFS patients and 11 matched controls, baseline augmentation index and carotid-radial pulse wave velocity did not differ; controls showed a 7.2% fall in AIx75 48 h after maximal cycling that was absent in ME/CFS (abstract numbers partly garbled).
reason: Measures arterial stiffness (AIx75, PWV), not FMD or PORH, and finds no baseline difference; no atlas finding covers arterial stiffness or post-exercise vasodilation, and the sample is very small.

result: Of 42 Charité patients with fatigue 6 months after mostly mild COVID-19, 41 had PEM and 19 met CCC for ME/CFS; CCC-positive patients had more fatigue (p=0.006), more frequent and longer PEM (p=0.003) and lower handgrip force (Fmean2 p=0.034) than non-CFS patients; MBL deficiency in 22% and raised IL-8 in 43%.
reason: Referred clinic cohort without uninfected controls, so not an incidence measure; it is the baseline of the Charité CCC cohort in trials-post-covid-course and also has grip data; earlier version of the same study as PPR309572.

result: Aptamer (SomaScan) profiling of 4790 plasma proteins in 20 female ME/CFS patients and 20 controls found 19 differing proteins implicating extracellular matrix, immune and ephrin signalling, with ROC AUC above 0.85 (up to 0.95 with protein ratios).
reason: Does not address the Hoel serum cell-leak artefact; a small SomaScan cohort with extracellular-matrix signals belongs with the cross-cohort plasma proteome findings, though the abstract names no individual proteins and the cohort may already be part of the meta-analysed set.

result: Pathway and cluster analysis of 19 differing plasma proteins in 20 vs 20 women highlighted the ephrin-Eph pathway; AUC above 0.85.
reason: Observational pathway-level signal, not Mendelian randomisation, and the abstract does not name EPHB1 or CLEC3B or give a direction, so it cannot be judged against the MR finding; covered by the retarget of the same paper.

result: In 278 ME/CFS patients (174 with and 104 without fibromyalgia) and 30 controls, pain, fatigue and concentration ratings rose after head-up tilt and stayed elevated at 7 days in patients only; fatigue and concentration peaked immediately, pain at 24 h.
reason: Same measure (post-exertional symptom time course) and adds orthostatic stress as a trigger with multi-day duration; the immediate peak for fatigue partly qualifies the 'delayed onset' part of the claim (also relevant to neuro-nonphysical-triggers if that id exists).

result: A systematic review of 18 physiotherapy RCTs (3 chronic fatigue, 14 CFS, 1 PEM-required ME) found that any intervention effects disappeared with narrower case definitions, more objective outcomes and longer follow-up.
reason: Extends the PACE critique (Oxford criteria, self-report only, effects fading with follow-up) across the wider exercise-therapy RCT literature.
